failure_patterns.pattern: strength_mismatch: Chose a vague or truncated option over the exact one: a bare conclusion without its derivable conditional clause, 'a subset of the tableaux' instead of the exact tableaux, 'cannot remain bounded' instead of finite-time blow-up.

rejected_edits.content:
11. Typed rider audit (do this for the 2-3 options that survive step 4; judge each differing clause by its type, not by whether it looks stronger or safer):
   - (R1) Deviation from the stem: 'even without hypothesis H', a different set than the stem defined (a bigger set T replacing the stem's Λ), a sub-range carved out of the stem's stated range, a closed vs open endpoint. Compare the option literally with the stem. A hypothesis the stem states is there to be used, so 'even without it' is false unless you can prove it. A carved-out sub-range is a weakening of a full-range statement.
   - (R2) Conditional rider 'if H then C': check directly that H implies C, and pick the H that is exactly sufficient. Weaker properties (generically injective, finite onto its image, birational, 'at least one of the two inequalities', total mass instead of a mass function) usually do not give pointwise or global conclusions. A stronger property (separates points, injective, embedding, both inequalities) does. A rider whose hypothesis demonstrably implies its conclusion is a derivable extra and BEATS the bare option that stops before it.
   - (R3) Added structure (free factor, a basis compatible with products across all degrees, an 'iff for every parameter', a decorated object): run a cheap invariant (rank or dimension count, size of a free factor vs the ambient rank, growth rates, degenerate parameter). If you cannot make it pass, reject the option however 'strong' it looks.
   - (R4) Vague weakening of a conclusion that the same hypotheses give in sharper form ('cannot remain bounded' vs finite-time blow-up; 'a subset of X' vs X; 'some threshold' vs the explicit threshold; 'exists' vs 'equals'): reject the vague option if the sharper option passes R1-R3. Choosing the vague option needs a named failure of the sharper one, and 'it feels safer' is not a failure.
   Then rank survivors by implication and take the strongest survivor.
rejected_edits.target: The answer is the pivot between 'true but weaker' and 'sharper but unjustified'.

rejected_edits.content: Burden of proof is symmetric. If you pick the more specific option, you owe a derivation or invariant test for its extra clause (typed audit R1-R3). If you pick the plainer, vaguer or weaker option, you owe the exact extra clause of the runner-up and the concrete test it fails (a counterexample, an invariant violation, a hypothesis that does not imply the conclusion). Never justify the weaker pick by 'the other adds something I cannot fully verify' when its added clause is the standard consequence of the stated hypotheses (R2) or the sharper form of the same conclusion (R4). Never justify the stronger pick by 'it is stronger' when its added clause has no derivation (R3), deviates from the stem (R1), or contradicts a small case. Also check that the strongest-looking option does not make a claim that is false for some parameter allowed by the stem (for example n>=3 when the stem says n>=2).
rejected_edits.target: ## Final sanity pass (do this before committing)

rejected_edits.content: - Stem-echo check: list the objects, sets and ranges the stem names (e.g. 'for every K and every p in (-1,inf]', 'the admissible set Λ', 'n>=2'). The faithful option reuses exactly these. Options that substitute another set (T for Λ), split the range into sub-ranges with an arbitrary cut-off, exclude a point, or add 'even without the hypothesis' are altered statements. When the stem itself says 'for every X and every p in R', the answer typically quantifies over all of R. Equally, 'strongest statement for every ...' is usually an 'always can / always holds' statement on the full stated class, not an 'iff' variant defined on a bigger parameter set.
rejected_edits.target: ## Near-duplicate options: constants, quantifiers, ranges, exact details
